prompt: During early germination, what is the main role of stored seed reserves before the seedling is fully photosynthetically independent?
options: They provide substrates and energy for resumed metabolism and early growth
They permanently replace mineral uptake by roots
They determine the final sex of the plant
They prevent all water loss from the embryo
explanation: Stored reserves in seed tissues are mobilized as metabolism resumes, supporting embryo growth and establishment before expanding photosynthetic tissues can supply most current carbon demand.

prompt: Why can a persistently saturated root zone reduce oxygen availability around roots even when the irrigation water itself contains dissolved oxygen?
options: Gas diffusion through water-filled pore space is much slower than through air-filled pore space
Roots stop respiring whenever water is present
Dissolved oxygen automatically converts to carbon dioxide at the media surface
Root hairs physically block all oxygen movement after irrigation
explanation: When pores remain water-filled, atmospheric oxygen replenishes the root zone much more slowly. Root and microbial respiration can then consume oxygen faster than it is replaced.

prompt: Which statement best describes source–sink integration in the vascular system?
options: Photosynthate moves through phloem from exporting source tissues toward importing sinks according to changing plant demand
Xylem transports sugars downward while phloem transports only water upward
Every leaf exports the same amount of carbon to every organ at all times
Sink tissues are always mature leaves and never developing organs
explanation: Source and sink status changes with development. Mature photosynthetic tissues commonly export assimilates, while growing shoots, roots, flowers, seeds, and storage tissues can act as competing sinks.

prompt: What best describes the role of vascular cambium during secondary growth in a cannabis stem?
options: It produces additional vascular tissues that contribute to radial thickening
It converts mature leaves directly into stem tissue
It is the main site of pollen production
It replaces the root system after flowering begins
explanation: Vascular cambium is a lateral meristem. As secondary growth proceeds it contributes new secondary xylem toward the inside and secondary phloem toward the outside, increasing stem thickness.

prompt: Which statement correctly compares major supporting tissues in a mature Cannabis sativa stem?
options: Bast fiber bundles occur toward the stem periphery while the inner xylem-rich core becomes more lignified
Bast fibers occur only inside the pith and xylem occurs only in the epidermis
All stem support comes from water pressure and no cell walls contribute
Bast fibers are reproductive tissues that develop only after pollination
explanation: Cannabis stems contain cellulose-rich bast fibers associated with outer phloem regions and a more lignified xylem-rich inner core. Their position, cell-wall composition, and maturation all contribute to mechanical behavior.

prompt: What is the main physical idea behind cohesion-tension transport in xylem?
options: Transpiration and water-potential gradients place a cohesive water column under tension from leaves toward roots
The stem pumps water upward using rhythmic muscle-like contractions
Phloem pressure forces all xylem water downward
Water moves upward only when roots generate positive pressure
explanation: Transpiration lowers water potential toward the leaf end of the pathway. Cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to conduit walls allow tension to be transmitted through the xylem water column.

prompt: Why can an embolized xylem conduit reduce stem hydraulic conductivity?
options: Gas occupying part of the conduit interrupts the continuous liquid pathway used for water transport
Gas permanently turns the conduit into phloem
Embolism increases the number of functioning water columns in every case
An embolized conduit immediately stops photosynthesis in every leaf on the plant
explanation: When gas fills a xylem conduit, that conduit loses part or all of its ability to conduct the continuous water column. Whole-stem impact depends on how much of the hydraulic network is affected and on plant context.

prompt: Why should branch angle be interpreted together with branch diameter, load, attachment geometry, and support rather than as a single strength score?
options: Mechanical failure depends on interacting geometry, tissue properties, leverage, and load
Branch angle has no relationship to canopy architecture
Only internode color determines branch strength
All branch attachments carry identical loads regardless of position
explanation: A branch is a loaded structure. Its risk of bending or failure depends on leverage, attachment, tissue condition, branch dimensions, supported mass, movement, and external support—not one angle alone.

prompt: What is the most important distinction between an axillary bud being present at a node and that bud producing an elongating branch?
options: A bud can already exist while its outgrowth remains suppressed until developmental and environmental signals permit activation
Every visible axillary bud must immediately become a branch
Axillary buds form only after the main shoot is removed
A dormant bud is actually a root primordium waiting to move into the soil
explanation: Axillary meristems and buds can be established without immediately elongating. Bud release and sustained branch growth depend on interacting developmental signals, light, resource status, and competition with other growing sinks.

prompt: Which statement best reflects current general plant evidence for control of axillary bud outgrowth?
options: Auxin, cytokinin, strigolactone, sugars, light, and sink competition interact; apical dominance is not a one-hormone on/off switch
Auxin simply flows from the main stem directly into every bud and permanently closes it
Only sugar concentration controls branching and hormones have no role
Bud outgrowth is determined entirely by branch angle
explanation: Modern branching models integrate several mechanisms. Auxin in the main stem acts indirectly, cytokinin generally promotes bud activity, strigolactone generally represses it, and sugar/light/resource relationships can influence whether released buds sustain growth.

prompt: How should node number and phyllotaxy be used when reading Cannabis development?
options: As developmental observations that can shift with genotype and conditions, not as a universal fixed-node clock for every Cannabis plant
As an exact species-wide calendar in which every cultivar changes phyllotaxy at the same numbered node
Only to diagnose root diseases
As proof of cannabinoid potency
explanation: A complete-life-cycle Cannabis study documented node-associated changes such as axillary buds, stipules, reproductive structures, and a transition from opposite to alternate phyllotaxy in its studied genotype. Those observations are useful references, but they should not be generalized into a fixed universal node number for all genotypes and environments.

prompt: Why should results from a pruning treatment in one Cannabis study not be converted into a guaranteed yield rule for every grow?
options: Architecture response depends on genotype, treatment type, timing, plant scale, environment, and the production goal
Pruning always doubles yield in every genotype
Removing the apex permanently stops all lateral growth
Branch removal cannot change canopy light distribution
explanation: Cannabis pruning experiments show real architectural plasticity, but treatments and genotypes do not respond identically. The Atlas therefore uses study results to explain mechanisms and observed responses rather than promising a universal yield outcome.

prompt: Why can leaf temperature differ from measured room air temperature?
options: Leaf energy balance includes radiation absorbed, convective exchange, and evaporative cooling through transpiration
Leaves always remain exactly two degrees warmer than air
Only root-zone pH determines leaf temperature
Leaf temperature is independent of light, airflow, and transpiration
explanation: Leaves exchange energy with radiation, surrounding air, and water vapor. Light load, airflow, stomatal behavior, humidity, and water status can therefore make leaf temperature diverge from air temperature.

prompt: Why is photoperiod response not identical to the first day that visible flowers appear?
options: Photoperiodic signaling and meristem transition precede many externally visible stages of flower development
Plants perceive photoperiod only after mature flowers have formed
Visible stigmas are the organ that measures night length
Photoperiod affects roots but not shoot development
explanation: Developmental signaling and meristem reorganization occur before all floral structures are externally obvious. Visible flower development is therefore a later observation in a broader transition process.

prompt: In a glandular cannabis trichome, where does much of the secreted resin accumulate relative to the secretory disk cells?
options: In a subcuticular storage cavity beneath the expanded cuticle
Inside xylem vessels in the trichome stalk
Only inside the nucleus of each secretory cell
Inside root hairs before transport to the flower
explanation: Secretory disk cells produce specialized metabolites that accumulate in a subcuticular storage space as the cuticle separates and expands over the gland head.

prompt: What distinguishes pollen contact with a stigma from successful seed development?
options: Pollen must progress through compatible reproductive processes leading to fertilization before embryo and seed filling can proceed
Any pollen grain touching any leaf immediately becomes a mature seed
Seed filling occurs before fertilization
Stigmas transform directly into embryos after contact
explanation: Pollen arrival is only an early step. Successful fertilization must occur before embryo development, reserve accumulation, seed-coat maturation, and later physical seed maturity.

prompt: When estimating plant-level vapor-pressure conditions, why is measured leaf temperature often more informative than assuming it equals air temperature?
options: Saturation vapor pressure at the leaf surface depends on actual leaf temperature, which can differ from room air temperature
Air temperature is never relevant to plant physiology
Leaf temperature alone determines root-zone EC
Relative humidity automatically forces leaf and air temperatures to be identical
explanation: Leaf temperature can diverge from air temperature because of radiation, convection, airflow, and transpiration. That difference changes the vapor-pressure gradient at the leaf surface.

prompt: Why should a repeated trait across one cultivar not automatically be treated as a universal deficiency or disease symptom?
options: Genotype, developmental stage, environment, and their interaction can produce repeatable phenotypes that are not a single pathological cause
Every visible difference is caused by the same nutrient
Genetics only affects seed color and cannot affect plant form
Environmental context becomes irrelevant once a cultivar name is known
explanation: Plant phenotype reflects genotype, environment, development, and their interaction. Diagnostic reasoning therefore needs baselines, comparisons, measurements, and progression rather than a universal visual label.
